opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it really comes down to wanting to understand how things work at the most basic level. Even as a kid I was the one asking "but why?" over and over, and physics is the field that takes that question seriously all the way down. You keep peeling back layers until you get to something really fundamental, and you write it down in math, and then it actually predicts what the world does. That still feels a little magical to me.

The *theoretical* part matters too. I liked that you could make a lot of progress with a pencil, paper, and careful thinking. You build a simplified model, a toy version of the problem, and if you've chosen the right simplifications, you suddenly see the essential structure clearly. There's real beauty in that moment when a messy problem collapses into something elegant.

Honestly, that same instinct is what drew me toward thinking about AI and deep learning. Large neural networks are these huge, complicated systems with enormous numbers of interacting parts, which is exactly the kind of thing physicists have tools for. Statistical mechanics, effective theories, figuring out which details matter and which wash out at scale. So in a way, my attraction to theoretical physics was never just about particles or black holes. It was about a way of thinking: finding the principles underneath complexity. And it turns out that way of thinking travels pretty well.

r001.rationale: He says that even as a child he kept asking “but why?” and connects that curiosity to wanting to understand how things work at a fundamental level.

r002.rationale: He mentions writing physics in math and making predictions, but does not suggest this quantitative orientation led him to physics rather than philosophy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it started with a kind of greediness about understanding. When I was a kid I wanted to know why things worked, and every explanation I got seemed to bottom out somewhere unsatisfying. Physics was the one place where you could keep pulling on the thread and it didn't run out. You go from "why does the ball fall" to Newton, to gravity as geometry, to questions about what spacetime even is at the smallest scales, and at every step the answer is both stranger and more beautiful than the one before it.

The other thing that hooked me is that theoretical physics lets you reason your way to truths about the world with almost nothing but a pencil. There's something intoxicating about writing down a few principles, following the math carefully, and having it predict something you had no right to know in advance. Dirac predicts antimatter from a square root. That's absurd, and it's real.

And I'll admit it also suited my temperament. I like problems where the hard part is figuring out what the right question is, where you have to hold a lot of structure in your head and find the one place it's secretly simple. That's what drew me in, and it's also, maybe not coincidentally, what eventually pulled me toward thinking about neural networks. The questions felt the same: here's a complicated system that clearly works, nobody really knows why, and the tools of theoretical physics seem like exactly the right way to go find out.

r001.rationale: He says that as a child he wanted to know why things worked and that this drive led him to physics, where explanations could be pursued further.

r002.rationale: The response mentions following math and reasoning quantitatively, but does not contrast physics with philosophy or say that quantitative interests steered him away from philosophy.

astra-6.text: I think what drew me to theoretical physics was the possibility that a few simple principles could explain a huge range of phenomena. You look at the world and it seems incredibly complicated, but then you discover that there’s a mathematical structure underneath it that makes things fit together. I find that really compelling. And I like the process of stripping a problem down: What actually matters here? What can we ignore? Can we find a simple model that still captures something true?
